defects.why: The Arabic word 'ملاحظات' means 'notes' or 'observations', but the English title uses 'Ḥuqūq' which means 'rights'. This is a completely different word and changes the meaning of the title.
defects.english: 2 – Ḥuqūq fī tarbiyah al-banāt

defects.why: The Qur'anic verse is left untranslated in the English text, so non-Arabic readers receive no meaning of this central ayah.
defects.english: «وَمَا خَلَقْتُ الْجِنَّ وَالْإِنسَ إِلَّا لِيَعْبُدُونِ»

defects.why: The English text leaves the Qur'anic verse in Arabic without providing an English translation, so the meaning is not conveyed to English readers.
defects.arabic: قُلْ إِنَّ صَلَاتِي وَنُسُكِي وَمَحْيَايَ وَمَمَاتِي لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ
defects.english: قُلْ إِنَّ صَلَاتِي وَنُسُكِي وَمَحْيَايَ وَمَمَاتِي لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ

defects.why: The English adds a source attribution not present in the Arabic, and the attribution is incorrect: this hadith is narrated by Muslim, not al-Bukhari.

defects.english: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Whoever dies knowing that there is no god but Allah will enter Paradise.' (Narrated by al-Bukhari).

defects.why: The Qur'anic verse is left untranslated in the English text, so its meaning is not conveyed to an English reader. The translation should provide an English rendering or at least a gloss.
defects.english: «وَلِلَّهِ الْأَسْمَاءُ الْحُسْنَىٰ فَادْعُوهُ بِهَا»

defects.why: The Arabic says 'avoid exposure to psychological stress' without specifying who is exposed. The English adds 'them' (children) and changes the meaning to avoiding causing stress to children, whereas the Arabic likely refers to the parents avoiding stress themselves.
defects.english: and to avoid subjecting them to psychological pressure

defects.why: The Arabic says something 'helps you as a father' to raise your children, but the English changes the actor to 'you can support', altering the meaning from being helped to doing the supporting.
defects.arabic: كثيراً ما يساعدكم كأب على تربية أطفالكم الصغار
defects.english: As a father, you can often support your *tarbiyah* (nurturing) of your young children

defects.why: The Arabic 'مقابس الأمان' in this context likely means seat belt buckles/sockets, not electrical safety sockets. The English 'safety sockets' is a literal mistranslation that changes the meaning to electrical outlets. Should be 'seat belt buckles' or 'safety belt sockets'.
defects.english: safety sockets

defects.why: The Arabic says 'لمجرد رؤية الآخرين له' meaning 'just so that others see it' (i.e., showing off), but the English says 'merely because others have it', changing the motive from ostentation to envy or keeping up with others' possessions.
defects.arabic: يحذر من شراء سيارة أو جهاز لمجرد رؤية الآخرين له
defects.english: It warns against buying a car or a device merely because others have it

defects.why: الترهيب means warning or instilling appropriate fear of consequences, not 'gentle discipline'; the translation softens and changes the intended method.
defects.english: Tarbiyah through encouragement and gentle discipline

defects.why: The Islamic term 'tarhib' is translated away instead of being transliterated or accurately rendered, inconsistent with the transliteration of Tarbiyah, murabbi, and akhlaq in the same document.
defects.english: gentle discipline

defects.why: The Arabic structure 'يجب على الوالدين أن يكونا... وأن يحرصا...' makes both actions obligatory. The English uses 'must' for the first but 'should' for the second, weakening the obligation to a recommendation.
defects.arabic: وأن يحرصا على الدعاء لهم بالخير والرحمة
defects.english: and they should be keen to make du'a for them with goodness and mercy

defects.why: The Arabic 'على الأب أن يختار' expresses a duty or obligation upon the father. The English 'should choose' reduces this to a suggestion, altering the deontic force.
defects.arabic: على الأب أن يختار زوجة صالحة قوية
defects.english: The father should choose a righteous and strong wife

defects.why: The Arabic says 'toward the maids/servants' (i.e., directing daughters to be with or rely on maids), not 'becoming like servants.' The English adds 'becoming like,' which changes the intended meaning.
defects.english: pushing their daughters toward becoming like servants

defects.why: The Arabic includes 'المظهر' (appearance) as an object of focus alongside tight or short clothing; the English omits it, changing the meaning.
defects.arabic: مع التركيز على المظهر واللباس الضيق أو القصير
defects.english: while focusing on tight or short clothing

defects.why: The Arabic explicitly says 'hit them gently' (ضربهم بلطف), which is a direct paraphrase of the hadith about commanding children to pray at seven and hitting them at ten. The English 'discipline them gently' softens and omits the specific action of hitting, altering the religious ruling.
defects.arabic: ويمكن ضربهم بلطف إن لم يلتزموا بها في سن العاشرة
defects.english: and may discipline them gently if they do not adhere to it by the age of ten

defects.why: The hadith is quoted in Arabic without an English translation, so its meaning is not conveyed to English readers; the source Arabic also quotes it, but a translation should render it.
defects.arabic: «من كان يؤمن بالله واليوم الآخر فليقل خيرًا أو ليصمت»
defects.english: «مَنْ كَانَ يُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ فَلْيَقُلْ خَيْرًا أَوْ لِيَصْمُتْ» (left untranslated)

defects.why: The Arabic pronoun 'كان موجوداً' most likely refers to the child (الطفل), meaning the child inherits from the waqf if the child is in existence (e.g., born alive at the time of entitlement). The English 'if one exists' is ambiguous and likely read as referring to the waqf, changing the condition.
defects.arabic: أن الطفل يرث من الوقف إذا كان موجوداً
defects.english: that the child inherits from a *waqf* (endowment) if one exists

defects.why: The Arabic says the children recite it (يقرؤونه), but the English makes the subject 'those who teach' also the one who recites, changing who performs the recitation and thus the condition for the reward.
defects.english: those who teach their children the Qur'an and recite it

defects.why: The Arabic word عنف means 'violence' and should be translated into English. Transliterating it as 'Unf leaves the title unintelligible to English readers and is not an Islamic technical term requiring transliteration.
defects.english: without 'Unf

defects.why: The Arabic uses 'عليه السلام' for Prophet Ibrahim, but the English uses 'ﷺ', which is reserved exclusively for Prophet Muhammad. This alters the honorific and is religiously incorrect.
defects.english: Prophet of Allah, Ibrahim ﷺ

defects.why: The Arabic explicitly says hitting/striking (الضرب), but the English uses the euphemism 'physical correction', which obscures the direct meaning and softens the instruction. This is a significant semantic shift in a parenting context.
defects.english: physical correction / Limited Physical Correction

defects.why: The hadith is left untranslated in the English text. The English reader cannot understand the teaching, so the core religious instruction is not conveyed. The translation should provide an English rendering of the hadith's meaning.

defects.english: «ليس المؤمن بالطعّان ولا اللعّان ولا الفاحش ولا البذيء»

defects.why: The Arabic uses the passive form 'يُوصى' (is advised), meaning the Prophet is the recipient of advice, not the giver. The English changes it to active 'advised', attributing a recommendation to the Prophet that the Arabic does not. This misattributes a statement to the Prophet.
defects.arabic: يُوصى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم بتطبيق نهج الرحمة على أطفالنا
defects.english: The Prophet ﷺ advised applying the approach of mercy to our children

defects.why: The Arabic idiom 'قضاء الحاجات' specifically refers to relieving oneself (toilet training/istinja), not general needs. The English is vague and loses the intended meaning.
defects.english: fulfilling needs

defects.why: The Arabic term 'muraqabah' (مراقبة) means mindfulness/awareness that Allah is watching, not literally observing Allah. The English 'observe Allah' is theologically incorrect and could imply watching Allah, which is impossible. It should be translated as 'mindfulness of Allah' or 'awareness of Allah'.
defects.english: observe Allah

defects.why: The Arabic 'تزكية للنفس' in this context means self-praise or self-commendation (claiming purity for oneself), not self-purification. The translation changes the meaning of the religious ruling.
defects.english: names that involve *tazkiyah* (self-purification) of the self

defects.why: Arabic refers to the child's peers, but English 'their peers' likely refers to the parents' peers, changing who the child imitates.
defects.english: their peers

defects.why: Arabic 'وحدة القيادة' means 'unity of leadership' (i.e., singleness/unified command), not 'unit of leadership' as a noun entity. The English changes the meaning.

defects.why: The Arabic preposition 'على' means 'upon/on', indicating that children are to be raised to possess patience and endurance. The English 'with' suggests the parents' manner of raising, changing the core meaning from teaching children patience to being patient as a parent.
defects.english: raising children with patience and endurance

defects.english: «Bada al-Islam ghariban wa-sa-ya‘udu ghariban kama bada’a, fa-tuba li-l-ghuraba’»

defects.why: The Arabic uses 'ضربهم' (hit/strike them) from the hadith, but the English softens it to 'disciplined', obscuring the explicit command.

defects.english: and disciplined for it at ten if they neglect it

defects.why: Same error as title: 'التأديب' is disciplining, not 'adab'. The parenthetical '(manners)' reinforces the wrong meaning.

defects.why: The Arabic 'تأديبهن' means 'disciplining them', not 'tarbiyah' (upbringing). The English substitutes a different Islamic term, altering the hadith's wording and meaning.
defects.english: excels in their tarbiyah

defects.why: The Arabic means neglecting or missing the prayer, a serious sin; the English 'wasting time for prayer' suggests merely not using time efficiently for prayer, which is a different and weaker meaning.

defects.why: The English title is a transliteration of the Arabic, not a translation. It does not convey the meaning of the hadith or the subtitle 'The Virtue of Disciplining Children' to an English reader.
